# 5 Risk (continued)

## TYPES OF EXCESS RETURN (OR ALPHA) {#a}

Confusingly we now have a number of different definitions of excess return and alpha; which should we use? Ultimately, it depends on the preferences of the asset owner and what exactly they are looking for. Alpha, the excess return adjusted for systematic risk, is often described as the holy grail of investment management.

Various definitions of excess return are listed in Table 5.26.

**Table 5.26** Definitions of excess return

| Type | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Excess return | Excess return above the risk-free rate. The numerator of the Sharpe ratio. |
| Arithmetic excess | $(r - b)$ is the most common. Often confused with alpha. See Equation 4.24. |
| Geometric excess | $\left(\frac{1+r}{1+b}\right) - 1$. The technically correct definition of excess return. See Equation 4.25. |
| Regression alpha | See Equation 5.36. |
| Jensen's alpha | See Equation 5.42. Excess return adjusted for systematic risk. My preferred definition of alpha as opposed to excess return. |
| Three-factor alpha | See Equation 5.66. |
| Four-factor alpha | See Equation 5.67. |
| $M^2$ excess | See Equations 5.138 and 5.139 (arithmetic and geometric versions). |
| Skew-adjusted $M^2$ excess | Excess return adjusted for risk and skew preference. See Equation 5.143. |
| Adjusted $M^2$ excess | Excess return adjusted for risk and preferences of skew and kurtosis. See Equation 5.142, my strong preference for calculating performance fees. |
| Differential return | See Equation 5.141. |
| Net selectivity | See Equation 5.65. |
